notes: Eclipse Loop 2.0.0 A DSP and persistence audit of all 32 bundled plugins, and the fixes it found. The headline is the one you can hear: the saturators no longer alias. What aliasing is, and why it made things sound cheap When you distort a signal you create harmonics. Push hard enough and some land above what the sample rate can represent — and they don't disappear. They fold back down the spectrum onto frequencies that aren't harmonics of what you played. Harmonic distortion tracks the note and reads as warmth. Folded distortion sits still and reads as harshness, brittleness, that thin digital edge. Nothing in the code was wrong. It did exactly what it said. That's why it survived every correctness check the project has. Measured, not claimed Eclipse Drive was the worst case — its saturator runs at up to 25× pre-gain. Measured with a 5 kHz tone at 44.1 kHz: | Drive setting | Before | Now | |---|---|---| | 0.25 (light) | −27.3 dB | −106.3 dB | | 0.50 (medium) | −14.7 dB | −97.6 dB | | 1.00 (maximum) | −10.5 dB | −82.1 dB | At maximum drive the folded junk used to sit 10.5 dB below the music. It's now 82 dB below, for 1.3% of one CPU core and five samples of latency
